summary: Several mechanisms exist for multicast in layer 3 BGP/MPLS VPNs, and the documents define them as optional building blocks. This informational RFC picks a subset considered mandatory so implementations can interoperate and implementers and deployers know what to expect.

eli5.summary: A box of building toys has many parts. This says which parts everybody must have so toys from different makers can still fit together.

questions: which mvpn features must be implemented
subtitle: Which multicast VPN mechanisms every BGP/MPLS implementation should support, so that vendors can interoperate.

tldr.problem: The multicast BGP/MPLS VPN specification offers several alternative mechanisms for each building block but does not say which to implement, so implementations may support subsets that do not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares the alternatives for auto-discovery, S-PMSI signaling, C-multicast routing, encapsulation, inter-AS tunnels and BIDIR-PIM, and recommends a core set for every implementation.
tldr.outcome: BGP-based auto-discovery and S-PMSI signaling are mandated, and implementations support both BGP-based and full PIM peering for C-multicast routing. The rest are recommendations.

facts.label: C-multicast routing
facts.value: Support both BGP and full PIM peering

today: RFC 6517 is an Informational document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the multicast VPN specification in RFC 6513.

sections.title: Why a Mandatory Set Is Needed
sections.content:
The multicast specification for BGP/MPLS VPNs (RFC 6513) includes several alternative mechanisms for some of its required building blocks, but it does not say which are mandatory to implement. The result can be implementations that support different subsets that do not interoperate. That is a problem for the many operators with multi-vendor backbones.

This document uses the requirements already stated in RFC 4834 to study each approach and pick good candidates for a core set of mandatory mechanisms. It also discusses how existing deployments of early implementations (RFC 6037) can be accommodated. Implementing other, non-mandatory mechanisms is not ruled out.
sections.eli5: If every toy maker picks different parts, the toys will not fit together. So this document picks a core set of parts that everyone should build.

sections.title: Auto-Discovery and S-PMSI Signaling
sections.content:
For MVPN auto-discovery, RFC 6513 offers BGP-based discovery and a PIM-based one that runs over a shared P-tunnel. PIM discovery only works with shared P-tunnels, while BGP discovery places no limit on the tunnel type and keeps the control and forwarding planes independent. BGP discovery can also detect inconsistent shared-tunnel identifiers, which matters most between ASes. The recommendation is that BGP-based auto-discovery is mandated.

For S-PMSI switching signaling, the choice is a UDP-based TLV protocol or BGP. The UDP protocol is an extra protocol in the MVPN stack and needs an MI-PMSI, so a PE must join the P-tunnels of all PEs. BGP signaling does not, which lets a PE delay joining and reduces state on P routers. It also fits both inter-AS approaches. BGP is the preferred and mandated solution, though the UDP protocol can be an option with a per-VRF knob for coexistence during migration. The authors do not recommend extending it to new P-tunnel types.
sections.eli5: Routers need to find out who else is in the group and when to switch to a special delivery route. Using BGP, which is already there, is simpler than adding another protocol.

sections.title: Exchanging Customer Multicast Routing
sections.content:
RFC 6513 has four ways for PEs to exchange customer (C-) multicast routing: full per-MVPN PIM peering over an MI-PMSI, lightweight PIM peering, unicast PIM Join/Prune messages, and BGP.

  • Scalability. The PIM approaches need many PIM adjacencies and periodic refreshes, so processing cost grows with the number of PEs. BGP avoids periodic refreshes and, with Route Target constrained distribution (RFC 4684), only the interested upstream PE receives a C-multicast route. It can also offload work to route reflectors, which may then need dedicated resources.
  • P routers and inter-AS. The PIM approaches require an MI-PMSI. BGP does not, and it keeps ASes isolated in inter-AS option B, which PIM does not.
  • Security. BGP supports MD5 peer authentication, while no comparable mechanism for PIM between remote PEs had been fully described.
  • Join latency. PIM can reach a shorter best case, but under loss or load a lost Join can cost a multiple of the refresh period. BGP over TCP degrades more smoothly.

Because full PIM peering is already deployed (it is the mechanism of RFC 6037) and BGP has little deployment experience, implementations are recommended to support both the BGP-based and the full per-MVPN PIM peering mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Routers can tell each other who wants what by chatting constantly, which gets noisy with many routers, or by using BGP, which is quieter. Since nobody knows yet which is best in practice, everyone should support both.

sections.title: Tunnels, Inter-AS and BIDIR-PIM
sections.content:
Encapsulation. No restricting recommendation is made, but implementations should not unreasonably limit the data plane or force one technology on all VPNs at a PE. Implementations should support the P2MP variants of the encapsulations they already support for unicast: mLDP, P2MP RSVP-TE and GRE/IP-multicast. Ingress PE replication works over a unicast core but uses bandwidth poorly, so it is unlikely to be a long-term choice.

Inter-AS. RFC 6513 offers non-segmented tunnels, where ASBRs act like P routers, and segmented tunnels, which are stitched together by ASBRs. Segmented tunnels scale better and let each AS pick its own tunnel technology. Non-segmented tunnels help migration from RFC 6037. Implementations should support the segmented model and consider the non-segmented one.

BIDIR-PIM. Of three methods in RFC 6513, the recommended one is Partitioned Sets of PEs, which splits a VPN into sets of VRFs with a consistent view of the route to the rendezvous point. It needs upstream-assigned MPLS labels or one MP2MP LSP per partition. If it cannot be used, standard DF election over an MI-PMSI and VPN Backbone as the RPL are interim options.
sections.eli5: Different networks can build their own delivery tunnels and join them at the borders, which gives them more freedom. For the tricky two-way multicast, the networks are split into groups so that packets cannot go around in circles.

sections.title: Summary of Recommendations
sections.content:
The remaining sections cover two smaller points and then the summary. Implementations should support a co-located rendezvous point model, but MUST support deployments where no PE has to run a PIM RP function or a VRF MSDP instance, because all RPs sit in customer networks or CEs. They are also recommended to support the procedures of Section 9.1.1 of RFC 6513, "Discarding Packets from Wrong PE", to avoid duplicates. For existing deployments, per-VRF configuration knobs allow incremental migration.

The final list of recommendations is: mandate BGP auto-discovery; mandate BGP for S-PMSI switching signaling; support both BGP and full PIM peering for C-multicast routing; use Partitioned Sets of PEs for BIDIR-PIM; implement P2MP variants such as mLDP, P2MP RSVP-TE and GRE/IP-multicast; support segmented inter-AS tunnels and consider non-segmented ones; and meet the co-located RP and duplicate-avoidance points above.

The RFC says it raises no particular security considerations by itself.
sections.eli5: The final list says which parts every maker must include, which parts are good to have, and that a customer should be able to keep running its own meeting point instead of handing it to the provider.

cells: Support both BGP and full per-MVPN PIM peering
P2MP variants: mLDP, P2MP RSVP-TE, GRE/IP-multicast
